extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, literary critics, humor theorists, and writers/comedians interested in the theory of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic/philosophical criteria describing what makes things comic and how laughter functions socially and aesthetically. Useful for critiquing or constructing comic situations, characters, gestures, words and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is essentially human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside what is strictly human; you may laugh at an animal or an object only because of some resemblance to man or the human caprice that shaped it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laughing at a hat because of the human shape or use given to it; laughable effect depends on perceiving a human attitude or expression. Anti-pattern: treating non-human beauty/ugliness as inherently comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic requires momentary anesthesia of emotion (detachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce the whole of its effect, the comic demands something like a momentary anesthesia of the heart; its appeal is to intelligence, pure and simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: comic works presume indifference or emotional calm in the audience. If the audience is emotionally engaged (pity/affection), laughter is suppressed or requires suspension of those feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is social and needs an echo
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter appears to stand in need of an echo: it is always the laughter of a group and implies a kind of secret freemasonry or complicity with other laughers, real or imaginary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: jokes that fail in another culture because they refer to group-specific customs; solitary hearing of others' stories may not elicit laughter if you don't 'belong to the parish.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is a social gesture with corrective function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter must answer to certain requirements of life in common; it has a social signification and is a sort of social gesture which, by fear and humiliation, restrains eccentricity and inelasticity of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: see laughter as a mechanism by which society softens down mechanical inelasticity and enforces sociability. Not a moral endorsement—laughter is utilitarian (corrective) rather than purely benevolent.

rubrics_metrics.name: The laughable stems from mechanical inelasticity (rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element often consists of a certain mechanical inelasticity — habit, absence of elasticity of mind or body — where living pliableness is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a runner who falls because muscles continue movement despite changed circumstances; victims of practical jokes who behave like machines. In character: vice or fixed habit that simplifies and rigidifies a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is often accidental and exterior at first
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is therefore accidental: it remains, so to speak, in superficial contact with the person, brought about by external circumstance or human knavery (practical jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between comic incidents caused by external mishaps and those where the comic is internalized in character (see deeper forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness and habitual automatism as comic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A mind always thinking of what it has just done and never of what it is doing (absentmindedness) supplies inexhaustible opportunities for comic revelation; automatism and habit produce laughable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the absent-minded person repeatedly making practical mistakes; Don Quixote as systematic absentmindedness around a central idea. Authors exploit this 'recipe' for comic manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic increases when the cause is natural and traceable
rubrics_metrics.description: When a certain comic effect has its origin in a certain cause, the more natural we regard the cause to be, the more comic shall we find the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for construction: give clear, plausible origins for comic behavior (habit, passion) rather than arbitrary causes to heighten laughability; audiences enjoy tracing the life-history of an affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vice is externalized and schematic
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice capable of making us laugh is that which is brought from without like a ready-made frame (it lends its own rigidity instead of borrowing our flexibility); comic vices retain a simple, independent existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: comic characters often bear names or titles referring to the vice (le Jaloux) and remain types rather than fully assimilated tragic individuals. Use common-noun titles for comic pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic physiognomy: fixed grimace or stiffness
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable expression is one that will make us think of something rigid and coagulated in the wonted mobility of the face — a unique and permanent grimace that seems to promise nothing more than it gives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caricature magnifies latent tendencies; faces that suggest a single mechanical action (always laughing, always weeping) are highly comic. Contrast with expressive beauty that remains mobile and adaptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature reveals latent tendencies by exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of the caricaturist consists in detecting an imperceptible tendency and rendering it visible by magnifying it — making models grimace as they would at the end of their tether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration must appear as means, not as an aim: it should reveal the embryo of distortion. Mere over-exaggeration without following nature's inclination fails to be truly comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in movement and gesture: forms and rhythms matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic element appears in forms and movements where a mechanical stereotype or arrested mobility is perceived within gestures; form is the outline of movement and suggests a habitual action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: clown horseplay, comic walks, or repetitive gestures. When constructing physical comedy, emphasize the contrast between expected adaptable movement and observed mechanical repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in situations: involuntariness and momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: People laugh at a falling runner not because of the change of attitude but because his sitting down is involuntary — the mechanical continuation of movement where adaptation was required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design situations where characters fail to adapt (momentum or lack of elasticity). Distinguish voluntary silliness (less comic in this sense) from involuntary mechanical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in words: relaxed, dream-like reasoning and play on sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonings at which we laugh are those we know to be false but might accept as true in a dream — a logic lacking in tension; play on ideas can degenerate into play on words as relations become superficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: witticisms that are abridged reasonings, jokes built like dreams where meaning slips into sound. For verbal comedy, craft seemingly logical chains that collapse into absurdity or pivot on sound rather than sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic often invites sympathy first (relaxation) before humiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic character is often one with whom our body momentarily sympathises — we adopt his gestures and relax with him; that relaxation is a prelude to laughter, which then becomes corrective and humiliating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: effective comedy can first lower audience tension (invitational play) then reveal the corrective sting of laughter. Beware of sustaining only sympathy without the corrective edge if the goal is classical comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is not always benevolent or just; it punishes indiscriminately
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter, being a natural mechanism, goes off spontaneously, returns tit for tat, and is incapable of dealing separately with each individual case — it may strike the innocent and spare the guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing audience response, expect moral ambivalence: laughter's social- corrective function can be spiteful or misapplied; creators should be aware of potential cruelty in comic exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is both utilitarian (social correction) and aesthetic (pleasure in form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter unconsciously pursues a utilitarian aim of general improvement by emphasising inelasticities, and yet the comic also has an esthetic side since it appears when society and individual regard themselves as works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: a comic piece can be assessed both for its social-function (does it correct or regulate?) and for its artistic qualities (form, grace, caricature). Balance corrective purpose with aesthetic delight.
